name: Aconite Violet
lede: Aconite Violet is a dusty purple named for aconite, the poisonous monkshood plant, and catalogued by Robert Ridgway in 1912.

sections.title: A poisonous flower's purple
sections.body:
The name comes from aconite, the genus *Aconitum*, also called monkshood or wolfsbane, a plant better known for its poison than for its hooded purple flowers; the color name borrows only the flower [1].

Robert Ridgway listed it in his 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature*, plate XXXVII, hue 63″ [1]. His plates survive as scans of aged printed chips, so the screen swatch is an approximation [1]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary gives an earlier record, 1905, and the ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955 filed the name under block 223, moderate purple [2][3]. Its nearest named neighbors are [[faded-purple]] at 2.9 units and [[dusty-purple]] at 3.2, with [[viola]] a more vivid cousin and [[grey-purple]] a duller one [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds Aconite Violet in only 5 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.02 percent, as photographed [4]. That makes it one of the rarer named purples in the collection [4]. The dated matches run from 1600 to 1915, with no single painter or school favoring it [4]. Even its strongest match, a 1915 canvas, holds it in only about six percent of the picture [4]. The measurement is a computed color match on photographed canvases, not a pigment identification [4].

origin.first_recorded: 1905 (Maerz & Paul, cited 1930); listed by Ridgway, 1912, plate XXXVII
